newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ budget likely to be too bullish on growth - ANZ.
newsitem.headline: NZ budget likely to be too bullish on growth - ANZ.

text.p: ANZ Bank (NZ) Ltd on Wednesday forecast GDP growth of only 1.7 percent in the year to March 1998, while predicting that the budget due in two weeks would forecast the same growth rate at 2.9 percent.
The Treasury's Budget Policy Statement (BPS) produced in March saw GDP growth at 3.6 percent in the 1997/98 year.

Treasurer and Deputy Finance Minister Winston Peters will deliver the government's 1997/98 budget at 2.00 p.m. (0200 GMT) on June 26. The budget is the first under the National/New Zealand First coalition government formed in December last year.
The March BPS gave preliminary projections for the fiscal outlook, incorporating the coalition's expenditure plans.
ANZ said those projections were based on an identical economic outlook to that contained in the December Economic and Fiscal Update (DEFU).
"This economic outlook has proven optimistic in light of the generally subdued economic indicators to hand in the first part of 1997," ANZ's economists said.

They predicted the budget's forecasts for 1996/97 growth would match the 2.6 percent forecast in the BPS. However, they themselves are currently forecasting only 2.5 percent growth in the year to March 1997.
The actual data for the fiscal year just ended is due from Statistics New Zealand four days after the budget.

ANZ saw the budget lifting the March 1998/99 GDP growth forecast to 3.5 percent from the 3.1 percent picked in the BPS. Finance Minister Bill Birch on Tuesday outlined an even more bullish forecast, saying he expected growth of at least four percent in 1998/99. But ANZ forecasts just 3.2 percent.
Likewise, the bank saw only 3.3 percent growth in 1999/2000, but expected the budget forecasts to stick with the 3.5 percent projected in the BPS.
The ANZ economists said New Zealand's weak economic climate was likely to lower the surpluses projected in the budget, something which has been clearly signalled by Peters.

However, the government was likely to be conservative in revising down the economic growth outlook, leaving the balance of risks for actual surpluses over the next three years firmly on the downside, it added.
Despite this, ANZ said it believed that the government would not cut or defer its planned spending initiatives.
"We believe the spending programme detailed in the BPS will be maintained -- the credibility of the Treasurer and his coalition rests on the delivery of their spending promises."
Overall, ANZ economists saw the budget projections incorporating a slightly lower revenue track than assumed in the BPS, and a higher track for expenditure.
"This will generate weaker projected operating surpluses and a slower rate of public debt reduction for the next three fiscal years."
It said the weaker climate would knock a number of revenue sources, including company taxation, PAYE, GST receipts and the proceeds from the government's trading operations.
Similarly, it would be likely to lift some expenditure items such as unemployment benefits.

ANZ expected the budget to show operating surpluses of around NZ$2.9 billion for 1997/98 (against $3.3 billion in the BPS), $2.3 billion in 1998/99 ($2.6 billion) and $3.2 billion in 1999/00 ($3.5 billion).

ANZ saw the budget forecasting net public debt as a percentage of GDP at 24 percent in 1997/98 (versus 23.4 percent in the BPS), 21.8 in 1998/99 (21 percent) and 18.7 percent in 1999/00 (17.8 percent).

"Recent comments by the Treasurer regarding the likely magnitude of fiscal surpluses over the next two years appear to have been designed to prepare the market for a slightly weaker outlook than in the BPS," ANZ said.
